master_narrator.agency_handoff_prompt:
The table was silent. Not the good, tired silence of a job well done. The sharp, brittle silence of sixteen people who had been breathing the same recycled air for too long. Sixteen mugs rested motionless in the warm circle of firelight while the captured geode hummed beneath the floorboards. Elias watched them carefully. He observed the textbook cascade of an isolated group under stress: mitigating Isolated-Confined-Extreme (ICE) Third-Quarter cortisol cascades and autonomic hypervigilance through structured communal roast rituals and oxytocin vagal buffering. His duty was to archive the linguistic and epistemic memory of the sixteen so nothing true is lost. But currently, he was just trying to ensure they survived dinner.

The silence shattered as Ryn slammed a ladle down. Arguments overlapped instantly—engineering versus biology, safety versus discovery. Elias monitored the Third-Quarter isolation micro-stressors across sixteen polymaths, only to watch the entire table nearly mutiny because Kaio filtered soup stock through a sock. 

A sudden, cold weight settled in Elias's chest. His jaw clamped tight. The urge to withdraw into immovable, deadpan stubbornness clawed at his usual contemplative patience. He crossed his arms. The heavy wool of his sweater settled solidly against his ribs. He sat back in his chair, digging his heels into the wooden floorboards, refusing to yield to the chaotic noise.

Therefore, he lowered his arms slowly to his lap. Escalating the standoff meant abandoning the fragile fellowship. He picked up his slate instead, noting the exact friction coefficient of the room. 

"If you're complaining and no one is laughing," Elias said, his voice quiet but carrying perfectly over the din, "you're complaining wrong."

Elara looked over from the other side of the table. "What did you say?"

"I said," Elias replied, his eyes twinkling, "that we brought eight centuries of differential calculus across the stars, yet here we sit arguing whether a magnetotropic turnip filtered through a sock belongs to metallurgy or theology. Personally, I vote we butter it first."
